q: Robert Hooke's observation of cork cells in 1663 led him to describe them as:
opts: A. Tiny fluid-filled sacs
B. Little boxes resembling a honeycomb
C. Membrane-bound organelles
D. Transparent spherical units

q: Which of the following is NOT a tenet of the Cell Theory as formulated from the works of Schleiden, Schwann, and Virchow?
opts: A. All living organisms are composed of one or more cells
B. The cell is the basic unit of structure and function in organisms
C. All cells arise from pre-existing cells
D. All cells must contain a nucleus to carry out metabolic functions

q: The concept that 'cells arise only by the division of existing cells' most directly refutes which historical belief?
opts: A. Germ theory
B. Spontaneous generation
C. Endosymbiotic theory
D. Lamarckian evolution

q: According to the cell theory, which of the following statements is CORRECT?
opts: A. Only eukaryotic cells contain genetic material
B. Physiological processes such as metabolism take place within the cell
C. Cells can only exist as independent single-celled organisms
D. Cells are the basic unit of structure only, not function

q: Which of the following correctly distinguishes prokaryotic from eukaryotic cells?
opts: A. Prokaryotes have membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes do not
B. Prokaryotic DNA is naked and found floating in the cytoplasm
C. Prokaryotes have a defined nucleus enclosed by a nuclear envelope
D. Eukaryotes lack ribosomes whereas prokaryotes possess them

q: In prokaryotic cells, the flagellum differs from that of eukaryotes in that it:
opts: A. Is composed entirely of lipid molecules
B. Lacks the 9+2 fibrillae (microtubule) arrangement
C. Is enclosed within a membranous sheath
D. Is only used for nutrient absorption

q: In eukaryotic cells, transcription occurs in the nucleus while translation occurs in the cytoplasm. What is the functional significance of this separation?
opts: A. It allows simultaneous transcription and translation on the same mRNA strand
B. It enables post-transcriptional modification of mRNA before translation
C. It prevents ribosomes from accessing the nucleus
D. It ensures that only prokaryotes can perform gene expression

q: Eukaryotic cells are approximately how many times larger than prokaryotic cells?
opts: A. Two times
B. Five times
C. Ten times
D. One hundred times

q: Which organisms are exclusively prokaryotic?
opts: A. Fungi and protists
B. Bacteria and archaea
C. Algae and plants
D. Viruses and prions

q: The fluid mosaic model of the cell membrane describes the membrane as fluid primarily because:
opts: A. Water molecules freely pass through the phospholipid bilayer
B. Unsaturated phospholipids allow lateral drift of lipids and some proteins
C. Proteins are covalently bonded to the phospholipid tails
D. Cholesterol molecules make the membrane rigid at all temperatures

q: Intrinsic (integral) membrane proteins differ from extrinsic (peripheral) proteins in that they:
opts: A. Are found only on the outer surface of the membrane
B. Span the entire width of the membrane
C. Combine exclusively with glycolipids to form glycoproteins
D. Function only as chemical receptors for hormones

q: The approximate composition of the cell membrane by percentage is:
opts: A. 45% protein, 45% lipid, 10% carbohydrate
B. 60% protein, 30% lipid, 10% carbohydrate
C. 50% phospholipid, 40% protein, 10% steroid
D. 70% lipid, 20% protein, 10% carbohydrate

q: Cholesterol affects membrane fluidity in a dual manner. At body temperature it:
opts: A. Increases fluidity by separating phospholipid molecules
B. Lessens fluidity by restraining movement of phospholipids
C. Has no effect on membrane fluidity
D. Causes phospholipids to flip between membrane layers

q: Glycoproteins and glycolipids found on the cell surface primarily function as:
opts: A. Energy storage molecules
B. Chemical receptors and cell recognition markers
C. Structural components that replace phospholipids
D. Enzymes for catalysing membrane reactions

q: The term 'selectively permeable' as applied to the cell membrane means that:
opts: A. The membrane allows all molecules to pass freely in both directions
B. Only water molecules can cross the membrane
C. The membrane controls which substances enter and exit the cell
D. The membrane prevents all substances from exiting the cell

q: Phospholipids are arranged in a bilayer in which the hydrophobic fatty acid tails:
opts: A. Face outward toward the aqueous environment on both sides
B. Point inward away from water on both sides of the membrane
C. Are oriented randomly within the bilayer
D. Form covalent bonds with water molecules

q: The inner membrane of the mitochondria is folded into structures called cristae. What is the functional importance of these folds?
opts: A. They store DNA used for mitochondrial replication
B. They increase surface area for oxidative metabolism enzymes and ATP synthesis
C. They separate the matrix from the cytoplasm
D. They serve as attachment sites for ribosomes

q: The smooth endoplasmic reticulum differs from the rough endoplasmic reticulum in that it:
opts: A. Is larger in size and transports more proteins
B. Lacks ribosomes on its surface
C. Is only found in plant cells
D. Contains more DNA than the rough ER

q: The Golgi apparatus receives material from the endoplasmic reticulum and:
opts: A. Immediately destroys it using hydrolytic enzymes
B. Processes, packages, and dispatches it in vesicles; it is also involved in lysosome formation
C. Sends it directly to the nucleus for DNA replication
D. Converts it into glucose for cellular respiration

q: The nucleus is often called the control centre of the cell because:
opts: A. It synthesises all the cell's ATP
B. It contains DNA, which controls all cellular activities and inheritance
C. It is the largest organelle in all cell types
D. It is surrounded by the roughest endoplasmic reticulum

q: Euchromatin differs from heterochromatin in that euchromatin:
opts: A. Stains deeply and contains inactive DNA
B. Stains lightly and contains transcriptionally active DNA
C. Is found only in prokaryotic cells
D. Contains no histone proteins

q: Lysosomes are primarily involved in:
opts: A. Photosynthesis and oxygen production
B. Autolysis and digestion of bacteria, redundant organelles, and vacuole contents
C. Synthesis of lipids for the cell membrane
D. Providing structural support via protein filaments

q: The nucleolus within the nucleus primarily functions to:
opts: A. Replicate chromosomal DNA during mitosis
B. Manufacture ribosomes and act as a storage area for materials
C. Control the passage of materials through the nuclear pores
D. Synthesise ATP for nuclear activities

q: Chloroplasts and mitochondria share which of the following features?
opts: A. They are both found exclusively in plant cells
B. They both contain their own DNA and reproduce by dividing
C. They both have a single surrounding membrane
D. They both synthesise glucose from carbon dioxide

q: Which structural feature of the nucleus allows communication between the nucleus and cytoplasm?
opts: A. The nucleolus
B. The nuclear pores perforating the nuclear envelope
C. The cristae
D. The chromatin network

q: Ribosomes are sites of protein synthesis and may be found:
opts: A. Only attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum
B. Only free in the cytoplasm
C. Either attached to the rough ER or free in the cytoplasm
D. Exclusively within the nucleus

q: Which cytoskeletal element is composed of actin protein and is associated with cell movement and muscle contraction?
opts: A. Microtubules
B. Intermediate filaments
C. Microfilaments
D. Spindle fibres

q: Spindle fibres, which are critical in pulling chromosomes to opposite poles during cell division, are composed of:
opts: A. Microfilaments (actin)
B. Microtubules
C. Intermediate filaments
D. Collagen fibres

q: Intermediate filaments serve which primary function in the cell?
opts: A. Drive chromosome separation during mitosis
B. Facilitate cytoplasmic streaming and cell migration
C. Provide mechanical support and hold organelles like the nucleus in position
D. Form the basis of cilia and flagella

q: Centrioles are involved in cell division and locomotion via cilia and flagella. They are composed of a complex arrangement of:
opts: A. Actin microfilaments
B. Intermediate filaments
C. Microtubules
D. Phospholipids

q: The covalent bond formed between two monosaccharides during the synthesis of a disaccharide is called:
opts: A. Peptide bond
B. Phosphodiester bond
C. Glycosidic bond
D. Ester linkage

q: Cellulose and starch are both polymers of glucose, yet humans can digest starch but not cellulose. The reason for this is:
opts: A. Cellulose contains fructose monomers while starch contains only glucose
B. Starch has alpha (α) 1-4 glycosidic linkages while cellulose has beta (β) 1-4 linkages that human enzymes cannot hydrolyse
C. Cellulose is a branched polymer while starch is always linear
D. Starch is water-soluble while cellulose is not

q: The structural polysaccharide chitin is functionally important as:
opts: A. A storage polysaccharide in animal liver cells
B. A component of plant cell walls alongside cellulose
C. The exoskeleton material of arthropods and cell wall support in fungi
D. The main energy source for red blood cells

q: Sucrose is formed from which combination of monosaccharides?
opts: A. Glucose + Glucose
B. Glucose + Galactose
C. Glucose + Fructose
D. Galactose + Fructose

q: Glycogen is the animal equivalent of plant starch. In humans, it is stored primarily in:
opts: A. The kidneys and spleen
B. The liver and muscle cells
C. Fat tissue and bone marrow
D. The brain and heart

q: In a dehydration (condensation) reaction joining two monomers, what molecule is released?
opts: A. Carbon dioxide
B. Ammonia
C. Water
D. Phosphate group

q: A triglyceride (triacylglycerol) consists of:
opts: A. Three fatty acids attached to a phosphate group
B. Three fatty acids joined to glycerol by ester linkages
C. Two fatty acids and a phosphate group attached to glycerol
D. A glycerol backbone with three amino acid chains

q: Unsaturated fatty acids are typically liquid at room temperature because:
opts: A. They contain no hydrogen atoms in their carbon skeleton
B. Cis double bonds cause bending, preventing close packing of fatty acid chains
C. They have shorter carbon chains than saturated fatty acids
D. They contain phosphate groups that repel each other

q: Phospholipids self-assemble into a bilayer in aqueous solution because:
opts: A. The phosphate head is hydrophobic and seeks the interior
B. The fatty acid tails are hydrophilic and face the water
C. The hydrophobic tails orient inward away from water while hydrophilic heads face outward
D. Cholesterol forces the phospholipids into a bilayer arrangement

q: Cholesterol is classified as which type of lipid?
opts: A. Triglyceride
B. Phospholipid
C. Steroid
D. Wax

q: Lipids differ fundamentally from carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids in that they:
opts: A. Are the only biological molecules that contain carbon
B. Do not form true polymers from monomers
C. Cannot be used as an energy source by cells
D. Are found exclusively in animal cells

q: The primary structure of a protein refers to:
opts: A. The three-dimensional folding of the polypeptide chain
B. The unique linear sequence of amino acids joined by peptide bonds
C. The coiling of the polypeptide into alpha helices
D. The assembly of two or more polypeptide subunits

q: In sickle-cell disease, the substitution of valine for glutamic acid at position 6 of the beta chain of haemoglobin results in:
opts: A. A change in primary structure that alters tertiary and quaternary structure, reducing oxygen-carrying capacity
B. Complete absence of haemoglobin production
C. Overproduction of alpha chains with no functional consequence
D. Denaturation of haemoglobin at normal body temperature

q: Secondary protein structure is stabilised primarily by:
opts: A. Disulfide bridges between cysteine residues
B. Ionic bonds between charged R groups
C. Hydrogen bonds between repeating constituents of the polypeptide backbone
D. Covalent bonds between adjacent R groups

q: Quaternary protein structure is present in:
opts: A. Any protein with more than 100 amino acids
B. Proteins consisting of two or more polypeptide chains assembled into one macromolecule
C. Proteins that contain only alpha helices
D. Denatured proteins that have lost their native conformation

q: Denaturation of a protein refers to:
opts: A. The hydrolysis of peptide bonds by digestive enzymes
B. The irreversible synthesis of new peptide bonds
C. The loss of native conformation due to changes in pH, temperature, or salt concentration, rendering the protein biologically inactive
D. The phosphorylation of amino acid R groups

q: Haemoglobin exhibits which level of protein structure, and what is its subunit composition?
opts: A. Tertiary structure; one alpha and one beta chain
B. Quaternary structure; two alpha and two beta polypeptide chains
C. Secondary structure; four identical polypeptide chains
D. Primary structure; a single polypeptide with four heme groups

q: Chaperonins are molecules that:
opts: A. Degrade misfolded proteins in the cytoplasm
B. Assist in the proper folding of other proteins
C. Catalyse the hydrolysis of peptide bonds
D. Transport proteins across the cell membrane

q: A nucleotide monomer consists of three components. Which combination is correct?
opts: A. Amino acid + pentose sugar + phosphate group
B. Nitrogenous base + pentose sugar + phosphate group
C. Nitrogenous base + hexose sugar + phosphate group
D. Fatty acid + ribose sugar + phosphate group

q: DNA and RNA differ in their sugar components in that:
opts: A. DNA contains ribose while RNA contains deoxyribose
B. DNA contains deoxyribose while RNA contains ribose
C. Both contain deoxyribose but differ in their nitrogenous bases
D. DNA contains galactose while RNA contains glucose

q: The two strands of a DNA double helix are described as antiparallel. This means:
opts: A. The strands are identical and run in the same direction
B. The strands run in opposite 5' to 3' directions relative to each other
C. One strand contains purines only while the other contains pyrimidines only
D. The strands repel each other due to negative charges

q: In DNA base pairing, adenine always pairs with thymine and guanine always pairs with cytosine. These pairings are maintained by:
opts: A. Covalent phosphodiester bonds
B. Ionic interactions between charged bases
C. Hydrogen bonds between complementary nitrogenous bases
D. Ester linkages between the sugars and bases

q: The nucleotide base uracil (U) is found in RNA but NOT in DNA. What base does uracil replace in RNA?
opts: A. Adenine
B. Guanine
C. Cytosine
D. Thymine

q: Which of the following correctly lists the levels of biological organisation in ascending order of complexity?
opts: A. Organ → Tissue → Cell → Organism → Organ system
B. Cell → Tissue → Organ → Organ system → Organism
C. Tissue → Cell → Organ → Organism → Organ system
D. Cell → Organ → Tissue → Organ system → Organism

q: Cardiac muscle tissue differs from skeletal muscle tissue in that cardiac muscle is:
opts: A. Voluntary and found in the walls of internal organs
B. Involuntary and found exclusively in the walls of the heart
C. Voluntary and responsible for all body movements
D. Involuntary and found in blood vessel walls only

q: Epithelial tissue can be classified by two criteria. Which pair is correct?
opts: A. By colour and by organelle density
B. By cell shape (squamous, cuboidal, columnar) and by number of cell layers (simple, stratified, pseudostratified)
C. By lipid content and by mitotic rate
D. By location in the body and by neural innervation

q: Glial cells in nervous tissue primarily function to:
opts: A. Generate and transmit electrical impulses across the body
B. Support and nourish neurons
C. Produce myelin sheaths around axons only in the central nervous system
D. Carry out phagocytosis of pathogens in the brain

q: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it:
opts: A. Requires ATP as an energy source
B. Moves substances against their concentration gradient
C. Requires transport (channel) proteins and is used for polar molecules that cannot cross the lipid bilayer freely
D. Only transports water molecules across the membrane

q: The sodium-potassium pump is a classic example of active transport. It maintains cellular ion gradients by:
opts: A. Pumping sodium into the cell and potassium out, using ATP
B. Pumping sodium out of the cell and potassium into the cell, using ATP
C. Allowing sodium and potassium to diffuse freely down concentration gradients
D. Using vesicles to transport ions across the membrane

q: Receptor-mediated endocytosis differs from pinocytosis in that it:
opts: A. Involves engulfing solid particles by wrapping the membrane around them
B. Takes in bulk quantities of specific substances via receptor proteins clustered in coated pits that bind a specific ligand
C. Is exclusively used for water uptake
D. Does not involve the formation of vesicles

q: Phagocytosis involves:
opts: A. A cell gulping tiny droplets of extracellular fluid into small vesicles
B. Receptor proteins binding specific ligands in coated pits
C. A cell engulfing a solid particle by wrapping its membrane around it, forming a vacuole that fuses with a lysosome
D. Vesicles from the Golgi fusing with the plasma membrane to secrete products

q: Exocytosis is a form of bulk transport where:
opts: A. The cell engulfs large molecules by forming new vesicles from the plasma membrane
B. Transport vesicles from the Golgi fuse with the plasma membrane to secrete cell products to the exterior
C. Substances diffuse passively down their concentration gradient
D. Ions are pumped across the membrane using ATP

q: A key difference between active transport and facilitated diffusion is that active transport:
opts: A. Uses channel proteins while facilitated diffusion does not
B. Always moves substances down their concentration gradient
C. Requires ATP and moves substances against their concentration gradient
D. Only occurs in plant cells

q: Chromatin is chemically defined as:
opts: A. DNA alone, coiled around a protein scaffold
B. DNA + basic histone proteins (low molecular weight) + acidic or neutral non-histone proteins (higher molecular weight)
C. RNA + ribosomal proteins forming the nucleolus
D. Pure DNA organised into 46 linear chromosomes

q: A metacentric chromosome is defined by the position of its centromere. In a metacentric chromosome:
opts: A. The centromere is at the tip, producing only one visible arm
B. The centromere is submedially placed, making one arm slightly longer than the other
C. The centromere is centrally located such that both arms (p and q) are of equal length
D. The centromere is way off to one side, creating a distinct long arm and short arm

q: The complete set of chromosomes in the cells of an organism is known as its:
opts: A. Genome
B. Genotype
C. Karyotype
D. Phenotype

q: During which phase of mitosis do all chromosomes align at the equatorial plane (metaphase plate)?
opts: A. Prophase
B. Anaphase
C. Metaphase
D. Telophase

q: The S phase of the cell cycle is characterised by:
opts: A. Protein synthesis and general cell growth
B. Final preparation and increased protein synthesis before division
C. Exact replication of each chromosome (DNA synthesis)
D. Physical separation of daughter cells

q: A kinetochore is a protein structure that appears at the centromere during prophase. Its primary function is:
opts: A. To synthesise new DNA strands during S phase
B. To serve as an attachment point for spindle microtubules, enabling chromosome movement
C. To dissolve the nuclear envelope at the start of prophase
D. To trigger cytokinesis after telophase

q: Which of the following cells does NOT undergo further division once it is mature?
opts: A. Bone marrow cells
B. Epithelial cells
C. Neurons and red blood cells
D. Intestinal lining cells

q: Meiosis generates genetic variation through which two mechanisms?
opts: A. Mutation and DNA repair
B. Random assortment of homologous chromosomes and crossing over between paternal and maternal chromosomes
C. Cytokinesis and spindle formation
D. DNA replication and transcription

q: The primary significance of meiosis in sexually reproducing organisms is:
opts: A. Production of genetically identical diploid daughter cells for growth
B. Reduction of chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n) in gametes, maintaining species chromosome number after fertilisation
C. Repair of damaged DNA in somatic cells
D. Generation of stem cells for tissue regeneration

q: Raunkiaer (1934) classified terrestrial vascular plants based on the position of their dormant buds. Plants classified as Geophytes have their buds:
opts: A. On shoot apices over 25cm above the soil
B. At or close to the soil surface covered by litter
C. Buried in underground structures such as rhizomes, bulbs, tubers, or corms
D. Spending their dormant period as seeds

q: Which of the following correctly describes the vegetation zonation of Nigeria from south to north?
opts: A. Sahel savanna → Sudan savanna → Guinea savanna → Rainforest → Mangrove
B. Mangrove → Rainforest → Guinea savanna → Sudan savanna → Sahel savanna
C. Rainforest → Mangrove → Guinea savanna → Sahel savanna → Sudan savanna
D. Guinea savanna → Mangrove → Rainforest → Sudan savanna → Sahel savanna

q: An estuary is best defined as:
opts: A. A cold, treeless region found in high latitudes
B. A zone of transition between a river and the sea, where fresh and salt water mix
C. A wetland characterised by waterlogged soils in the Niger Delta
D. A large coniferous forest found in the northern hemisphere

q: Derived savanna in Nigeria is ecologically significant because it represents:
opts: A. A natural savanna that has never been disturbed by human activity
B. A forest that has been transformed into savanna due to human activities such as land clearing, grazing, and fire
C. A transition zone between marine and freshwater habitats
D. The southernmost vegetation belt bordering the Gulf of Guinea

q: The principle of non-maleficence in bioethics refers to:
opts: A. Ensuring fair treatment and equity in all research situations
B. Respecting an individual's capacity to make informed, uncoerced decisions
C. The human obligation not to do harm, requiring identification of parties that may be harmed and steps to minimise that harm
D. Identifying who benefits from a good action and how those benefits are realised

q: The Tuskegee Syphilis Experiment (1932–1972) is cited as a pivotal reason why bioethics is important because it demonstrated:
opts: A. The effectiveness of penicillin in treating syphilis in African American men
B. That scientists may not recognise when their conduct is unethical, necessitating shared guidelines and oversight
C. That GMO research poses the greatest risk to human health
D. That animal experimentation is the primary ethical concern in biomedical research

q: Scientific misconduct includes falsification, fabrication, and plagiarism. Falsification specifically refers to:
opts: A. Making up data or other relevant information at any stage of the research process
B. Using another person's ideas or words without giving appropriate credit
C. Manipulating research materials, equipment, or processes, or changing/omitting data such that the research is not accurately represented
D. Failing to disclose conflicts of interest in peer review

q: Which ethical principle in bioethics refers to respecting an individual's capacity to make an informed, uncoerced decision?
opts: A. Beneficence
B. Non-maleficence
C. Respect for autonomy
D. Justice/Equity
